html:
The early farming and fishing peoples of the Korean Peninsula and southern Manchuria, labelled Koreans on the map in 2000 BCE. Their map shape reaches from the peninsula west to the Liao River.

Around 2000 BCE the peninsula was in the late Jeulmun pottery period, named after its comb-patterned pots. People lived in pit houses near coasts and rivers, fished, gathered shellfish and acorns, and were starting to grow millet. From about 1500 BCE the Mumun period brought plain pottery, rice farming, larger villages and bronze, and thousands of stone dolmens were raised over graves.

Later Korean tradition says that Dangun founded the first kingdom, Gojoseon, in 2333 BCE. This is a founding myth; historians date Gojoseon as a state to the first millennium BCE. Its successors led on to the Three Kingdoms of Korea.
